tasks.task_description: Part a: Build one or more model(s) that capture the flow of passengers through a US airport security checkpoint and identify the bottlenecks and problem areas in the current process (Zones A-D, the Pre-Check/regular lane split, and the effect of the ~45% Pre-Check mix).
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: discrete-event simulation (DES) of a 4-lane checkpoint group, modeled as two parallel M/G/c queueing pools (Pre-Check and regular). Rationale: the process is a serial chain of stations with human-paced, right-skewed service times and a rare heavy-tailed branch (pat-downs), which closed-form M/M/c cannot represent. The DES lets us keep the service-time tail (the source of wait variance) intact and read off P50/P90/P99 waits and the utilization rho that governs stability. The bottleneck is identified structurally: the Zone B divesting/binning table is the dominant, variable, single-server station - one passenger at a time, duration set by the traveler (shoe/belt/jacket/laptop/liquid removal) not by staff, so it cannot be speeded by adding officers. The X-ray belt and walk-through/millimeter-wave scanner run at a near-deterministic fixed mechanical pace and are rarely the constraint; the ID-check station (Zone A) is fast and staffed in parallel so it clears. Therefore each lane is a single server at Zone B feeding low-variance downstream stations, and the whole checkpoint's throughput is set by the lane that is most heavily loaded. The supplied 20-minute snapshot (58 Pre-Check + 47 regular arrivals) is used to calibrate the arrival mix: the data itself shows ~55% of arrivals are Pre-Check, higher than the 45% enrollment figure - the regime in which the problem's 'unexplained long Pre-Check lines' appear. Assumptions: (1) each lane is an independent single server at Zone B with exponential inter-arrivals routed by the traveler's lane choice; (2) the scanner (~6 s) and X-ray belt overlap with the passenger's body scan and add only a small residual, so they are not the binding constraint; (3) the checkpoint operates at its peak (a flight-bank surge), which is the regime that produces the observed variance; (4) passengers do not switch lanes once in line (the 'no-cutting' social norm, see part c).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: two lane pools, i in {pre, reg}, with c_i lanes (base case c_pre=1, c_reg=3, per the 1:3 staffing rule). Arrival process: non-homogeneous Poisson, total rate lambda(t) = lambda_mean * surge * envelope(t); at peak lambda_mean=0.03/s so lambda_peak=0.075/s (~4.5 pax/min, ~270/hr). Each arrival is Pre-Check with probability p_pre (base 0.45; dataset-observed 0.55) and joins pool i. Per-lane service time S = S_B + delta + S_scan + 1[alarm]*S_patdown, where S_B ~ Lognormal(mean S_B, CV 0.5) is the passenger-paced divesting time (regular 42 s, Pre-Check 20 s), delta is a cultural dead-time gap (part c), S_scan ~ 6 s, and 1[alarm] ~ Bernoulli(p_alarm=0.02) with S_patdown ~ Lognormal(mean 90 s, CV 0.4). Per-lane service rate mu_i = 1/E[S]. Utilization rho_i = (lambda_i / c_i)/mu_i with lambda_pre = p_pre*lambda_peak, lambda_reg = (1-p_pre)*lambda_peak. The DES routes each arrival to the least-loaded lane (earliest free) of its pool, recording the wait W = start - arrival. Outputs: mean, P50, P90, P99 wait and rho per pool. A pool is unstable (queue grows without bound) when rho_i >= 1. Data cleaning (stated repairs): the CSV mixes two timestamp encodings - HH:MM.S for the station process-time columns and M:SS for the 'Time to get scanned property' belt column - which were parsed to seconds separately; a trailing blank row and the sparsely-filled station columns (ID/X-ray have many NaNs from station sampling) were dropped. Cleaned: 58 Pre-Check + 47 regular arrivals; Pre-Check inter-arrival median 4.8 s (p90 24 s), regular 9.5 s (p90 27 s); belt-to-belt 28.6 s mean, 48 s p90.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At the fixed 1:3 lane split the Pre-Check lane, not the regular lanes, is the bottleneck. Base case (45% Pre-Check, peak 2.5x): Pre-Check rho=0.938, mean wait 92 s, P90 232 s; regular rho=0.685, mean 6 s, P90 23 s. Raising the Pre-Check mix to the dataset-observed 55% pushes the Pre-Check lane past stability: rho=1.147, mean wait 373 s, P90 555 s, while the regular lanes relax to rho=0.56 (mean 5 s). Sweep over p_pre at the 1:3 split shows the Pre-Check lane crosses rho=1 at p_pre about 0.51 - so any airport where more than about half the travelers are Pre-Check (common at hubs, and exactly the 55% in the supplied data) has a structurally unstable Pre-Check lane: a single Pre-Check lane carrying ~half the volume against a staffing rule that assumes 1/4. That is the primary problem area: the mismatch between the fixed 1:3 rule and the realized Pre-Check share. The regular lanes sit at comfortable utilization (rho 0.5-0.7) and are not the constraint; their waits are dominated only by the occasional Zone D pat-down. Limitations/biases: (1) the DES assumes passengers never switch lanes, so it slightly understates the ability of a regular traveler to escape a stalled Pre-Check line; (2) service-time means were calibrated to the expert's empirical ranges rather than the sparse station columns (only 9-11 usable ID/X-ray samples), so the absolute wait magnitudes carry the CV uncertainty of a Lognormal fit; (3) the snapshot is one 20-minute window, so the arrival mix is an estimate, not a day-long statistic. None of these change the qualitative conclusion that the single Pre-Check lane is the binding, variance-producing constraint.

tasks.task_description: Part b: Develop two or more modifications to the current process that increase throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model each to show its impact.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: each modification changes a parameter of the same DES (lane allocation, Zone B work content, or lane count) and is re-run at the same peak load, so the before/after is a controlled comparison. Four modifications are modeled. M1 (lane reallocation): replace the fixed 1:3 rule with a split proportional to the realized Pre-Check share - e.g. 2 Pre-Check + 2 regular when the mix is ~55%. M2 (reduce regular-lane divesting work): pre-staged bin stations, in-line 'what to remove' signage, and pre-boarding preparation messaging cut the regular Zone B time from 42 s to ~28 s. M3 (surge absorption): open an additional regular lane at peak (1 Pre-Check + 4 regular), using the expert's observation that lanes clear at the net service margin so a fifth lane drains a surge faster. M4 (combined): M1 + M2 together (2:2 split plus reduced regular divesting). Rationale: M1 removes the structural bottleneck (under-provisioned Pre-Check lane) and directly attacks the variance driver; M2 and M3 raise capacity; M4 shows the two levers are complementary. All keep the same safety standard because none removes a screening step - they change allocation and preparation, not security content.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same DES as part a, re-run with one parameter changed per scenario, holding lambda_peak=0.075/s, surge 2.5x, duration 7200 s, seed 0. M1: c_pre=2, c_reg=2, p_pre=0.55. M2: S_B_reg=28 s (from 42), c_pre=1, c_reg=3, p_pre=0.45. M3: c_pre=1, c_reg=4, p_pre=0.45. M4: c_pre=2, c_reg=2, p_pre=0.55, S_B_reg=28 s. Outputs: per-pool rho, mean and P90 wait, as in part a.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (Pre-Check | regular): base 1:3 @45%: (rho .938, 92 s, P90 232 s) | (.685, 6 s, 23 s). M1 (2:2 @55%): (.573, 7 s, P90 22 s) | (.840, 28 s, P90 86 s). M2 (1:3 @45%, S_B_reg 28 s): (.938, 92 s, 232 s) | (.492, 1 s, P90 5 s). M3 (1:4 @45%): (.938, 92 s, 232 s) | (.514, 1 s, P90 5 s). M4 (2:2 @55%, S_B_reg 28 s): (.573, 7 s, 22 s) | (.604, 7 s, P90 27 s). Interpretation: M1 is the single most effective change for the variance problem - it takes the Pre-Check lane from the unstable regime (rho 1.15, 373 s) to a comfortable .573 (7 s), at the cost of loading the regular lanes to .84 (still stable, P90 86 s). M2 and M3 alone do almost nothing for the Pre-Check wait because they only add regular-lane capacity; the bottleneck is the Pre-Check lane, so extra regular lanes are wasted on an already-underloaded pool (this is why 'just add more lanes/staff' failed to fix O'Hare - the extra capacity went to the wrong pool). M4 is the best combined fix: it balances both pools (Pre-Check .573 / regular .604, both mean ~7 s, P90 ~27 s), so both throughput and variance improve simultaneously and no pool is overloaded. Recommendation: reallocate lanes to the realized Pre-Check share (M1) as the primary lever, and add regular-lane divesting-efficiency work (M2) to keep the regular pool from becoming the new bottleneck once the split is balanced. Limitations: the fixed seed gives a single sample per scenario; the M1 regular-lane P90 of 86 s reflects the heavier regular load and is the residual variance to watch, which M4 removes.

tasks.task_description: Part c: Treat cultural norms / traveler style as a sensitivity analysis. Consider how personal-space norms, collective-efficiency vs individual-efficiency, and queueing/cutting behavior change how passengers process through the checkpoint, and how the system can accommodate these differences to expedite throughput and reduce variance.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: model the cultural difference as a change in how the queue feeds the divesting table, not as a change in the loading task itself. The expert's mechanism: personal-space and cut-avoidance norms add a dead-time gap delta between successive occupants of the table - the table idles for those seconds while the next traveler waits for a comfortable gap or declines to close up / cut ahead. This reduces the effective per-lane service rate by a factor delta/(S_B+delta), i.e. it lowers utilization headroom on an already-loaded lane. Three traveler styles are swept: close-packed / collective-efficiency (delta=0 s, table continuously occupied - the throughput-maximizing case), US-style personal space (delta ~3 s), and strong cut-avoidance / slower travelers (delta ~6 s). The accommodation lever is to decouple arrival spacing from table occupancy - pre-staged bins, a call-forward pacing that advances the next traveler the instant the table clears, and a single-file serpentine - so the dead-time gap is removed without asking travelers to abandon their personal-space norm.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same DES; the only change is the per-lane dead-time delta added to S (S = S_B + delta + S_scan + 1[alarm]*S_patdown). Swept at the stressed configuration (1:3 split, 55% Pre-Check mix, peak 2.5x) where the Pre-Check lane is near/over capacity, plus the base 45% mix. delta in {0, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8} s. Output: Pre-Check and regular rho, mean and P90 wait per delta.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At the 55% mix / 1:3 split the cultural gap is catastrophic for the Pre-Check lane but nearly free for the regular lanes: delta=0 -> (rho 1.147, mean 373 s, P90 555 s) | (rho .56, 5 s); delta=4 s -> (rho 1.312, 850 s, P90 1450 s) | (rho .605, 7 s); delta=8 s -> (rho 1.477, 1335 s, P90 2368 s) | (rho .65, 10 s). The asymmetry is the mechanism: a near-capacity lane (Pre-Check at rho ~1.1) converts even a 2-4 s idle gap into a large queue because there is no headroom to absorb it, while an under-loaded lane (regular at rho ~.55) absorbs the same gap with almost no wait increase. At the 45% mix (Pre-Check rho .94) the same gap moves the Pre-Check mean wait 92 s -> 151 s (delta 3 s) -> 360 s (delta 6 s) while regular stays at ~7-10 s. Accommodation: (1) pre-staged bin stations and clear in-line signage remove part of the table idle time for every style; (2) a call-forward pacing system that advances the next traveler the moment the table clears closes the personal-space gap for the table (travelers still keep their personal space in the queue, but the queue is a single-file serpentine that feeds continuously); (3) for hubs with high Pre-Check shares, allocate lanes by realized share (part b M1) so that the lane that is culturally slowed is not also the one over capacity. Net effect: decoupling arrival spacing from table occupancy plus demand-proportional lane allocation keeps both pools below rho ~0.8 across all three traveler styles, which is what expedites throughput and flattens the variance. Limitations: the cultural effect is parameterized by a single scalar delta (a reasonable one-dimensional proxy, but it lumps personal-space, cut-avoidance, and dexterity differences into one idle-time knob); the sweep uses the same fixed seed per delta, so the P90 at the unstable deltas (delta>=4 s at 55%) is a large-sample estimate of a diverging queue rather than a steady-state value.

tasks.task_description: Part d: Propose policy and procedural recommendations for security managers grounded in the model, globally applicable or tailored to culture/traveler type, and assess the model's strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: translate each validated model result into a concrete, low-cost operational rule, prioritizing levers that change allocation and preparation (which the model shows move the binding constraint) over levers that add capacity to the wrong pool (which the model shows are wasted). Recommendations are tagged by the sub-result they rest on.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations (each with the model evidence that supports it): (1) Reallocate lanes to the realized Pre-Check share, not the fixed 1:3 rule. Evidence: at 1:3 the Pre-Check lane crosses rho=1 at p_pre about 0.51, so any hub above ~50% Pre-Check is structurally unstable; a 2:2 split at 55% brings it to rho .573 (mean 7 s). This is the single highest-leverage, cheapest change (no new hardware, no extra officers - just open the right lanes). (2) Open an extra lane (or convert one regular to Pre-Check) whenever the realized Pre-Check share exceeds 50%, as a standing peak-hour rule. (3) Invest in regular-lane divesting efficiency (pre-staged bins, signage, pre-boarding prep) to hold the regular pool at rho ~0.6 once the split is balanced, so rebalancing does not create a new bottleneck (M2/M4 evidence: S_B_reg 42->28 s drops regular rho .84->.60). (4) Use single-file serpentine queues with call-forward pacing to remove the cultural dead-time gap at the table without compromising personal-space norms (part c: delta 0->6 s moves the Pre-Check mean 92->360 s at 45% mix; pacing closes that gap). (5) Tailor by airport type: at leisure airports (Pre-Check share <40%) keep the 1:3 rule and focus on surge absorption (open a 5th lane at peak, M3); at business hubs (Pre-Check >50%) the rebalancing rule is mandatory. (6) Staff for the net-margin drain: because lines build fast at a surge but drain only at the service-arrival margin, schedule the lane-count change ahead of the flight bank (predictable) rather than reactively, and keep one flexible officer who can staff a pat-down without pulling from a lane's divesting flow (part c Zone D: a pat-down that borrows an officer re-stalls a lane). Model strengths: (i) it reproduces the reported 'unexplained long lines' as a predictable structural effect (lane-count vs realized-mix mismatch) rather than a mystery; (ii) it separates the variance driver (the right-skewed Zone B service time + cultural idle gap on a near-capacity lane) from the mean (throughput), so the two objectives are addressed by different levers; (iii) it is a DES, so it keeps the service-time tail that drives P90/P99, which closed-form M/M/c would smooth away. Weaknesses: (i) the 20-minute snapshot gives the arrival mix only as an estimate and too few station samples to calibrate the ID/X-ray process times directly; (ii) the cultural effect is a one-scalar proxy; (iii) a single seed per scenario means no confidence intervals on the wait estimates. Future work: (i) collect a full-day, multi-airport station-level log to pin the service-time distributions and the true Pre-Check share by hour; (ii) add a queue-switching behavior term (regular travelers abandoning a stalled Pre-Check line) to capture the social norm that cuts both ways; (iii) couple the lane-allocation rule to a real-time arrival-rate forecast (flight-bank schedule + delay feed) so the rebalancing is triggered automatically; (iv) extend to a multi-checkpoint airport with shared officer pools to model the Zone D officer-borrowing stalls explicitly.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The recommendations are ordered by leverage-per-cost: lane reallocation (1,2) is free and removes the structural bottleneck; divesting efficiency (3) protects the regular pool after rebalancing; serpentine + pacing (4) is the cultural accommodation that reduces variance without new screening; airport-type tailoring (5) and surge-ahead scheduling (6) make the policy robust across the arrival-process regimes the model identified. Together they move both pools to rho < ~0.8 under the base, 55%, and all three cultural styles, which is the model's target for low variance with maintained throughput. The core insight for managers is that the problem is not a capacity shortage in the aggregate - it is a mismatch between a fixed lane split and a variable Pre-Check share, plus the conversion of small per-passenger idle times into large queues on the one lane that is already near capacity. Assumptions carried from parts a-c (passengers do not switch lanes; scanner/X-ray are not the binding constraint; the model is evaluated at the peak) apply to the recommendations; the main risk to the recommendation is that if the realized Pre-Check share were far below 40% (a small leisure airport), the 2:2 split would over-serve Pre-Check, so rule (5) gates it on the measured share.
